attempts.reply:
Tests on texts I wrote point to one broad pattern, though it is diffuse and the top examples look scattered, so my confidence is low.

- **Strongest cases:** the main verb of a goal or purpose phrase after "to", especially after a verb of movement. "He asked her to come to the house to **see** if she could help" reached 9.3, "came over to **thank**" 6.8 and "traveled to Rome to **visit**" 5.2. Verbs with a pending complement in legal or embedded clauses also fire: "that the school **admit** only boys" (5.7) and "take into **account**" (6.1).
- **It is not just predictability:** fixed phrases like "in spite of", "took advantage of" and "as a matter of fact" stayed near zero.
- **Weak or silent:** short, complete sentences ("The rain fell.", "Hello, my name is John…", a plain list of fruits) stay below about 1.5.
- **Code:** it also fires where a code expression is still open, such as `([`, `= [`, `= 0` or a colon introducing code ("look like:"), at roughly 3.5 to 5.5.
- **Ranks 51 to 500 partly fit:** many are verbs or prepositions inside clauses ("to **meet**", "the facts **show** that"). Many others are scattered mid-phrase nouns, word pieces, line breaks and code tokens, which is why confidence is low.

I'm calling it one broad job rather than unrelated ones. The weak point is that "an unfinished phrase" is loose enough to cover most of the scattered examples.

A "said" before the quote barely fired (1.0).
- **"of" inside a quantity phrase:** "more and more of" gave 7.2, but "Many of the students" gave about 0.1. So this one is inconsistent.
- **Numbers and symbols in structured text:** math expressions, ¶ legal citations and decimals gave moderate scores (3–5.4). Code dots were lower (2.8).

The common thread is loose: positions inside a clause where an object or the rest of a value is still to come.

**Candidates I tested:**
1. A category plural just before a list of examples ("artists like…", "dishes such as…", "Notable scholars included…").
2. Wording that spreads across many things ("here and there", "every drawer", "from place to place").

These turned out to be the same idea.

- **Unusual senses fire more:** within the set, the less common meaning tends to score higher. "May tree" scored 7.8 against 3.7 for the month, "can of worms" 5.9 against 1.0 for "you can", and "shall we?" 7.5 against 1.9 for "I shall return". The name Bill (8.3) beat a bill in the mail (5.7).
- **Lower ranks are looser:** past rank 200 the hits spread to John, son, brother, Bay and some commas, at about 5–6.

Since all of this follows the identity of the token, I'd call it one job, with medium confidence.

**What fires it.** It is strongest in fixed formal wording, including:
- **Legal and contract text:** "Licensor", "shall", "holding" in case citations, "unless otherwise stated".

attempts.reply:
I tested the main idea and read examples from ranks 51 to 439, which is enough to answer.

- **Main pattern:** the unit fires on partitive quantity phrases, the "some of the X" construction. It peaks on "of" after "Some", "Many" or "Most", or on the determiner after "of", in phrases like "most of the", "a lot of the", "much of the", "the majority of the" and "a large portion of the".
- **Test results:** "Some of my", "A lot of the", "A large portion of the" and "Most of the" scored 6.5 to 7.9. "None of", "Each of", "All of", "The rest of" and "a great deal of" were weaker, at about 2 to 3.4. Phrases where "of" doesn't pick out a share of a group, like "queen of England", "color of the sky" or "cup of the tea", stayed near 0. Plain "Some people" and "Most people" with no "of" stayed below 1.
- **Exceptions:** a few strong cases don't fit. Disclosure boilerplate ("this post may contain affiliate links") scored 6.7 when I tested it, and "the hard work" scored 6.2. The ranked list also shows "the very", "the following", citation numbers and code tokens, and these get more common lower down. They look like minor side activity, not a second clear job.

attempts.reply:
Testing is finished: I made 8 tool calls (6 activation tests, 2 example reads), and one pattern held up.

The unit fires on the word just before a pronoun that points back to something already mentioned, usually "it", "them" or "they". In other words, it fires when the next word is very likely to be such a pronoun.

The unit responds to forward-looking or uncertain statements: predictions, expectations and hedged guesses about what will or might happen. That one pattern covers nearly all the snippets, so I chose A, with medium confidence.

- **Strong hits:** A full sentence making a prediction lit it up. "we can **expect** another heavy defeat" scored 9.5, "will **doubtless** appeal" 7.3 and "**probably** much higher" 6.3.
- **Modal words:** "will", "could", "may", "would", "sooner or later" and "if" all scored about 3 to 5 in short prediction sentences.
- **Non-predictive uses stay low:** Plain past-tense stories, a historical fact and a receipt all stayed at or below 0.6. "will" as a noun and "May" as a month did not fire either.

I read these as information that tells the reader what to expect, so I counted them as part of the same pattern. If you treat them as a separate genre, B is the alternative answer, which is why I didn't say high confidence.
- **Ranks 51–500:** These mostly fit. Remaining exceptions are a few code tokens (like the `=` in snippet 35), citation numbers and odd single words that don't fit any clear pattern.

- **Ordinary prose stays near zero:** news, recipes and everyday sentences all scored 1.0 or less.

**Lower-ranked examples:** ranks 51–70, 200–219 and 400–419 show the same mix: PHP, citation markers, number series, legal opinions, travel guides, plot and review text, and Japanese subtitles. The confidence is medium rather than high because these could all be text types from particular sources, which would make the patterns somewhat related. I had no way to test that.

**Candidate tested:** the slot right after "with", "using" or "use" when it introduces an instrument or means. The 50 snippets mostly fire on the token just after such a cue, often "a", "his" or "your".

**What the measurements showed:**
- **Strong when the context is clearly instrumental, peaking on the token just after the cue:**

  - "Use your head" scored 7.7 on "your".
  - "using a spoon" scored 7.9 on "a".

I'd call this unit **B (related jobs)**, with medium-to-low confidence. It fires in the middle of fixed, formula-like phrases, but it covers several distinct clusters rather than one clean pattern.

**What I tested and found:**
- **Legal citations:** the "." in "F.2d" or "P.2d" scored 7.6 when it followed a case name like "Smith v. Jones". The same "." scored only about 1.4 in a bare citation list, so it seems to depend on that context.
- **Joining two names:** "et al." scored 5.7–6.5 and "Le Roi et l'Oiseau" scored 6.0. "Ben & Jerry's" scored 4.3, "Tom and Jerry" 4.7 and "Romeo and Juliet" 4.2. Plain "et" in a French sentence barely registered (1.5).
- **Unit exponents:** the "1" in "g L^−1" and "mg kg^-1" scored about 7.
- **Abundance or variety phrases:** "a wide range of" (8.5), "a broad variety of" (9.5), "just about everything" (6.5) and "something for everyone" (4.3).
- **Controls:** ordinary sentences stayed near 0. So did other predictable set phrases ("in order to", "as well as", "United States of America"). That rules out "any highly predictable next token" as the explanation.
- **Ranked examples 51–500:** these show the same mix, plus scattered noise: IDs, hex codes, math notation and phrases like "enough … to" or "the opportunity".

The clusters loosely share one theme (a fixed, conventional phrase that is only partway through), but I couldn't find a single rule that predicts all of them.

attempts.reply:
I'd call this unit **C (unrelated jobs)**, with medium confidence. Its strongest and most reliable trigger is the middle piece of a long word split into several tokens, but at least three other triggers have nothing to do with that.

1. **Middle of a split word or identifier (strongest).** Rare names fire hard: K**oc**henberger 7.9–8.9, G**aug**uin 7.9, K**oz**lowski 7.6, G**ug**genheim 7.1–7.4, T**uro**ver 6.6. Rare ordinary words do too, like "indent**ured**" (5.5) and "trans**ester**ified" (5.7). Underscores and pieces inside code constants also fire: DB_VERIFY_BAD 6.5, APPLICATION_JSON 5.6, AF_INET 4.8. Rubidium-type cases fire as well, such as "Rub" in a shop name (6.0).
2. **Turning down an offer.** "No thanks**,**" scored 8.1 and "Thanks **but**" 7.5. "**politely** refused" scored 6.8, and the words after it kept firing. "Unfortunately we must decline" got only 3.2, and a "Sorry, I can't help" line barely fired (1.3).
3. **The line break right after a photo credit.** Credits like "(Supplied: …)" and "Getty Images" fired about 4 on the following newline. A plain paragraph break (1.8) or a "Photo credit: Reuters" line (0.7) didn't.
4. **"the court" in legal writing**, especially just before a ruling: 4.1–4.6 before "denies" or "will grant", but about 1.2 before neutral phrasing like "finds that".

Facets 2–4 reached only about half the strength of the original examples in my tests. The ranked examples from 51 to 500 were just as scattered, so a single description won't predict this unit well.

- **Weaker, unconfirmed cases:** "a bit of" (6.2), mid-word pieces in fixed phrases (ADJ-UD-GED, 5.5), and paragraph breaks after quoted dialogue. My dialogue test only reached about 2.3, so that last one is the least supported.

What links them may be that the unit fires where the next words are a specific item the context has set up, but that is my reading, not something I measured. The lower-ranked examples are mixed, which is why confidence isn't higher.

I'd call this unit **A (one job)**, with medium confidence.

**What I tested:** I started with one candidate: verbs and prepositions that place an entity somewhere, or move it through, to or past a place. I tested it with 30 texts over 6 probe calls and read 60 ranked examples (ranks 51–70, 100–119, 200–219 and 420–439).

- **Strong hits match the top snippets.** These are travel-guide style route sentences: "Buses from Inverness… and Thurso stop in Helmsdale" (7.2 on "stop"), "the Manchester–Sheffield line passes through the village" (5.4), "Trains… call at Linlithgow" (4.8). Other spatial predicates also fired: "was based in Cambridge" (4.5), "He lived and worked here" (5.3), "bone ingrowth into the component" (4.9 on "into").
- **Non-spatial sentences stayed near zero.** "approved the budget", "wrote a letter", "Prices rose sharply" and "She ate a sandwich" all came in at or below 0.3.
- **Context matters.** "Ferries for Orkney leave from Scrabster" reached only 0.4 as a bare sentence. In its original setting it reached 3.9 on "from", and the 4.5 peak moved to the distance phrase "two miles west". The same phrase "based in Cambridge" scored 0.5 in one sentence and 4.5 in another, so the wording alone doesn't decide it.
- **Two top snippets didn't reproduce.** The strongest snippet, "the man who inspired them", gave only 1.7 (on "who"), and "contact him" gave 0.6. These look like weaker, non-spatial edges of the pattern rather than a second job.
- **Lower ranks get loose.** Ranks 51–119 mostly fit (stops, landed, stayed, climb into, rode past, 500 meters away). By ranks 200–439 the examples are diffuse and the activations are lower (about 4.6–5.4), so the pattern is clearest near the top.

I'd label this unit B (related jobs), with medium confidence. It fires where the text points ahead to a value or object being compared against, ruled out or extended along a scale.

**Two main patterns**
1. **"any" covering a whole set.** It fires on "any" after verbs and prepositions such as "outweighs any", "rejected any", "met any burden", "thank you for any help" and "larger than any".
   - My tests confirmed this: "Thank you for any help" reached 10.0, "outweigh any risks" 7.5 and "better than any other phone" 6.0.
   - Ordinary "any" stays quiet: "if you have any questions" scored 0.1 and "I don't have any money" 2.5 (peaking on "money", not "any"). Sentence-initial "Any person who…" was weak at 1.9.
2. **The link to the next number in a range or list.** It fires on "to", "and", "or even" or a comma before the next value.
   - "4GB to 8GB" scored 8.7, "25,000 or even 50,000" 8.7, "between 20 and 30" 6.5, and the "and" before the last dose in "10, 20, 40 and 80 mg" 7.2.

**A related third group: words of comparison or overriding**
- Words like "than", "beat", "outweigh", "supersede" and "replace" also fire: "supersede" 6.1, "beat" 4.8 and "than" 3.5–4.6.
- I read this as the same idea of measuring something against a scale or set, which is why I chose B rather than C.

**Why not A**
Ranks 51–500 have a long tail of unrelated hits, including math solutions after a newline, code tokens, the French "cendres" (8.1 when tested) and citation page numbers. The core patterns are clear, but the unit isn't purely one job. That noise is also why my confidence is medium rather than high.

attempts.reply:
I'd call this unit B (related jobs), with low confidence. Its strongest responses fall into a few clusters that share one theme, technical or structured notation, but it also fires weakly across ordinary prose. That spread makes a single "one job" label hard to defend.

- **Email addresses:** this was the strongest pattern. It peaks on the first token of the username after "Email:" or "<", for example "dr", "mr", "se" and "r". My own test texts reached 11.9, above the top shown snippet.
- **Algebra drills:** it fires on the "*" between a coefficient and a variable, rising to about 9 later in the expression. It also fires on repeated items such as "sqrt(84".
- **Statistics tables:** it fires on decimal digits inside parentheses, ± values or confidence intervals, such as "11.[3]" and "(0.2--3.[8])".
- **LaTeX and markup:** it fires on tokens like "\partial", "Sl[ash]", subscripts and "xsl:[with]".

Ranks 51–500 were much more mixed. Many of these were mid-sentence words in formal, legal or scientific prose ("[implied]", "Iowa, [United]", "[involved]"), mostly at about 5–7.

Two ideas didn't hold up when I tested them:
- **Predictable next token:** counting sequences, weekday lists and "Obama… United" stayed below 3.
- **Repetition alone:** "red apple" repeated five times stayed at 1.2.

Python code and casual narrative prose stayed low (0.5–2.1), as did nonsense text (0.5).

attempts.reply:
I'd call this unit **B (related jobs)**, with medium confidence. It does two related things: it fires just before a boolean value in code, and it fires in prose that lists alternatives, variants or kinds of something.

**Candidates tested**
1. **Code, right before a true/false value.**
   - **Fires strongly:** `updated = false` gives 7.5 on the `=`. `return true` gives 8.9 on `return`, and `return false` gives 6.6. `checked="true"` gives 5.4 on `="`.
   - **Stays low:** a numeric assignment (`total = 0`) stays below 1.4, and `return x + 1` gives 0.4. So it's predicting a boolean, not reacting to assignments in general.
   - **Weaker without context:** short snippets like `settings.debug = false` only reach 2 to 3.
2. **Prose that counts kinds or alternatives.**
   - **Fires:** "lists three dialects" gives 6.0 to 4.7. "two varieties… red form and white form" gives 6.1. "contains at least" gives 5.9, and "There is also a white variety" gives 5.2.
   - **Weaker:** plain "there are many flowers" only reaches 2.4.
   - **Stays low:** neutral sentences stay below 1.5.

**Ranked examples (ranks 51 to 470)**
- They fit both patterns: `Enabled = true`, `return false`, "at least two", "four major groups", and many "There is/are…" sentences.
- They also include `==` comparisons and `setOpaque(false)`.
- By rank 450 and below, the examples are much more scattered (e.g. "of", "into", "but"), so the unit is less predictable at low activation.

**Why B rather than A or C**
Both patterns seem to be about choosing among a small set of options. "yes vs. no" fires at 4.6 and "either true or false" at 3.0. Still, code booleans and listing kinds of things in prose look like two separate jobs that share that theme, not one pattern. "Either stay home or go out" only reached 2.9.

messages.text:
I'd call this unit **B (related jobs)**, with medium confidence. It does two related things: it fires just before a boolean value in code, and it fires in prose that lists alternatives, variants or kinds of something.

**Candidates tested**
1. **Code, right before a true/false value.**
   - **Fires strongly:** `updated = false` gives 7.5 on the `=`. `return true` gives 8.9 on `return`, and `return false` gives 6.6. `checked="true"` gives 5.4 on `="`.
   - **Stays low:** a numeric assignment (`total = 0`) stays below 1.4, and `return x + 1` gives 0.4. So it's predicting a boolean, not reacting to assignments in general.
   - **Weaker without context:** short snippets like `settings.debug = false` only reach 2 to 3.
2. **Prose that counts kinds or alternatives.**
   - **Fires:** "lists three dialects" gives 6.0 to 4.7. "two varieties… red form and white form" gives 6.1. "contains at least" gives 5.9, and "There is also a white variety" gives 5.2.
   - **Weaker:** plain "there are many flowers" only reaches 2.4.
   - **Stays low:** neutral sentences stay below 1.5.

**Ranked examples (ranks 51 to 470)**
- They fit both patterns: `Enabled = true`, `return false`, "at least two", "four major groups", and many "There is/are…" sentences.
- They also include `==` comparisons and `setOpaque(false)`.
- By rank 450 and below, the examples are much more scattered (e.g. "of", "into", "but"), so the unit is less predictable at low activation.

**Why B rather than A or C**
Both patterns seem to be about choosing among a small set of options. "yes vs. no" fires at 4.6 and "either true or false" at 3.0. Still, code booleans and listing kinds of things in prose look like two separate jobs that share that theme, not one pattern. "Either stay home or go out" only reached 2.9.

{"label": "B", "description": "Fires right before a boolean value in code (`x =`, `return`, `flag:` before true/false), and in prose that lists alternatives or variants (\"there are two forms/varieties\", \"at least\", \"yes vs. no\").", "confidence": "medium"}

attempts.reply:
About 46 of the 50 snippets, and almost every later-ranked example I read, share one pattern: the unit fires on a token that sits partway through something unfinished, where what comes next is tightly constrained.

**Candidates I tested:**
1. **Next token is easy to predict in general.** This is wrong. "Once upon a time", "United States of America", "toothbrush" and "the quick brown fox" all scored about 0.
2. **Fragments inside rare or long words.** This holds up strongly:
   - "irrep[ress]ible" 8.1
   - "un[utter]able" 7.8
   - "Batalin-V[il]kovisky" 7.8
   - "circumn[av]igation" 7.5
   - "indec[ipher]able" 6.7
   - "B[ail]rigg" 8.4
   - "Category:[Writ]ers" 10.2
   - "R[us]kin" was lower (2.8), and "C. elegans" was weak (3.1), probably because "elegans" came out as a single whole-word token.
3. **Function words in the middle of fixed or idiomatic phrases.** This also holds:
   - "hard pill [to] swallow" 7.6
   - "as far [as]" 6.8
   - "not even [worthy] [to]" 5.1 / 5.9
   - "too heavy a burden for me [to] bear" 5.2
   - "can't [even] guess" 5.2

   It needs a marked, set-phrase setting. Ordinary "I want to go" scored 0 and "too tired to walk" scored 1.1. The "to" in a range follows the same rule: in the style of a statistics paper ("95% CI -2.96 to 5.96") it scored 8.0, but plain "10 to 20 meters" scored 0.1.

**Smaller forms of the same thing:** pieces of math or LaTeX left open (`}{`, `(`, `^`, `$\`), decimal points between digits, and partial URLs or code names. These fire more weakly, mostly 2–7. In my own math test they reached only about 2.5, and decimals about 2.5–3.4.

**Ranks 51–500:** these fit too: "ar[ach]noid", "in[el]uctable", "Comp[uls]ory", "E[ile]an Donan", decimals, `}{`, "takes two to". So I'm treating it as one broad pattern, not several jobs. Confidence is medium because the pattern is abstract and the function-word and math cases are less consistent than the word fragments.

**Candidate I tested:** someone's life talked about as a thing with its own fate. The strongest hits are when "life" is the subject and on the verb that follows it.

**What I measured:**
- **Strongest:** "Doctors said his life was not in danger" peaked at 10.7 on "was", with "life" at 8.7 and "not" at 8.9. "Their lives changed forever" gave 6.9 on "lives", "Your life will never be the same" 6.4, "Life is beautiful" 7.0 on "is", and "The tree's life span" 7.5 on "life".
- **Weak when "life" is the object:** "He saved her life" gave 1.2 and "She lived a long life" gave 2.0. "I love my life" was in between at 4.0.
- **Similar time spans also fire, but less:** reign plus "was cut short" (6.7 on "cut"), "Her career was in danger" (8.0 on "was"), "marriage was falling apart" (5.8), "The game was over" (5.3), "His tenure as CEO was brief" (5.4).
- **Endings on their own:** "ground to a halt" fired strongly (7.9). But "He disappears and never returns" and "lost following its destruction" stayed near zero, so ending language alone isn't enough.
- **Controls:** unrelated sentences stayed at or below 1.1. "Battery life" was weak at 2.6, and "his health was not in danger" was moderate at 3.4.

**Ranked examples beyond the 50 snippets:** ranks 51–70 are still mostly "life" or something lasting a set time: "normal life", "Life continues", "your life started", "minimum stay", "the season is well over", "the episode closes". They read as low-level noise rather than a second job, which is why I didn't choose B or C.

I'm calling this unit **B (two related patterns)**, with medium confidence.

**Pattern 1: "in" adverbial phrases.** The unit fires on "in" and the word after it when they start a sentence adverb or a time phrase.
- "In any case/event" is the strongest: up to 7.5 in my tests, and 10.0 for the top snippet.
- Season and month phrases also fire, such as "weekends only in October" (6.9 on "in"), along with "in the future" (4.8) and "In other words" (3.8).
- It is specific to "in". "At any rate", "On the other hand", "By the way" and "In fact" all stayed near zero. So did plain locative "in the box".
- It fires more when a sentence comes before it ("In addition" scored 2.1 that way, about zero on its own) and in travel-guide text.

**Pattern 2: the middle of a fixed name.** It fires on a piece inside a multi-token proper name or set compound:
- "Sar|ap|en" (6.1), "S|amp|els" (6.6), "Ow|ain" (4.0)
- "Washington Post" (4.5), "San Francisco Chronicle" (4.1), "Manchester Metropolitan" (3.7), "National Park" (3.6)
- London postcodes like "W1" (3.4)

**Why I linked them:** in both cases the unit fires inside a stock multi-word unit whose continuation is easy to predict. That link is my reading, not something I tested directly. Ranks 51–420 fit these two groups, with some odd extras (math commas, code tokens). Confidence is medium because the two patterns could be separate jobs.

attempts.reply:
I'd call this unit **B (related jobs)**, with low confidence: it has two clear patterns, and its weaker examples are scattered.

1. **Section openers in formal writing (the main pattern).** It fires on the heading or phrase that starts a new section or step of reasoning in legal, scientific, mathematical and patent text.
   - Examples: "ANALYS|IS", "CON|CLUSION", "Proof", "Introduction", "Upon review", "by induction", "the following".
   - My tests scored 5–7.4 for "Proof", "IV. CONCLUSION", "Introduction", "Upon review" and "the following sources:".
   - Context matters. The same heading words score low in casual text (a recipe's "Directions" got 2.2, "Conclusion" in a chatty trip post got nothing) and in plain running text ("Based on the foregoing analysis" got 1.4).
   - Some headings are weak: "Methods" and "Results" scored about 1.6–2.7, while "Discussion" reached 4.5.

2. **The later piece of some fixed compound terms.**
   - Strong: "401(k" (6.3–8.1), "hyper|activity" (7.0), "anger-|management" (6.2), "head-|over" (5.4), "home |away" (5.1).
   - This is selective. "state-of-the-art" scored 1.2, "Tilt-A-Whirl" 2.0, "post-traumatic stress" 2.1 and "double-blind, placebo-controlled" nothing.

The link between the two is loose: both look like a highly predictable next piece within a set formula. Beyond the top-ranked examples, the list (ranks 100–470) is quite mixed, with dialogue, code lines and generic nouns as well as these two patterns. That mix is the main reason my confidence is low.
